CAFETERIA LESSON · CAFETERIA · AGES 2–5 YEARS

Lemonade — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches lemonade through the body’s own comedy — the sour-face pucker — and lets the child mix the real thing from three ingredients.

What is this?

Lemonade is lemon juice, water and sugar stirred together and served cold, usually with ice and a lemon slice on the rim. It is sour and sweet at the same time.

What does it mean?

Point to the lemonade is a search among drinks — and lemonade is the trickiest, since milk, water and lemonade all pour. The lemon slice on the rim is the tell.

What does the child need to know?

The pucker is the lesson: one small sip and the whole face reacts. Name it — sour! — and the child owns a taste word forever.

Why this matters

Sour is the last taste word children usually learn, and lemonade is its friendliest teacher — a sour that chose to be delicious.

What it teaches

Taste words, three-step stirring, and cold-temperature vocabulary.

Words to learn

lemonadesoursweetcoldicestir

Say this to your child

“Squeeze the lemon — push push! Sugar in, water in, stir. Now the sip... THE FACE! That face means sour! Sour and sweet together — lemonade! Can you make the face again?”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and find the lemon slice riding the rim. Mix the real thing: half a lemon squeezed by the child, a spoon of sugar, water, ice — stir and sip. Make the sour face together, then name it: sour! Then sweet! Then both at once. Finish by pointing back at the card and asking which taste lemonade has.

Look closer at the picture

Watch the face: eyes squint, lips pull — the pucker is involuntary and hilarious. Photograph it; the child will demand to see it.

Ask your child

What does lemonade taste like? What did we squeeze? What rides on the rim? Is it warm or cold?

What your child can say or do

Sour! / My face did it! / Sweet too. / Cold one.

Out in the real world

Lemonade stands are the classic first business of childhood — the child who has mixed the real thing runs a better stand and knows why it sells.

Try it together

Lemonade stand: set up three cups — water, sugar water, lemon water — and let the customer sip each and name the taste. The pitcher refills; the faces repeat.

Understanding check

Ask what lemonade tastes like. Sour, sweet, both, or a demonstrated pucker — all pass.

This lesson pairs with the Lemonade flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Cafeteria.
